messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam is a 21-year-old married man who came to treatment months after witnessing a violent assault on his younger brother outside their apartment building. He still cannot tell the story straight through. When he tries, the memory breaks apart into fixed images: his brother’s arm twisted at an unnatural angle, a bloodied hand on the pavement, the stunned stillness of a face he loves. What returns most vividly is not language but snapshots, along with the sharp smell of metal and exhaust that seemed to hang in the air while he knelt beside him waiting for the ambulance. Because the event lives in him this way, as pictures and smell more than words, Liam has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself anymore; he says his own mind will not do what it is supposed to do, and that the person he was before—steady, useful, able to act—has been lost.

In the weeks afterward, certain moments began to hit him with startling force. A stranger moving abruptly near him on the sidewalk, an offhand remark about someone’s family, even catching sight of an injured arm or hand on television or in public could pull him back toward that night. Those moments did more than upset him. He would feel immediately on guard when other people moved suddenly, as if danger were beginning again in front of him, and at times he would abruptly feel as though he were back outside the building with his brother on the ground. The triggers also pulled the memory closer in its sensory form: the image of body parts associated with the attack flashing in his mind, the smell returning without warning, the whole thing present as if he were looking at photographs rather than recalling a past event.

What frightened Liam most was that his body seemed to react before he could think. He had come to believe that his body was now his enemy, launching into alarm even when he knew he was technically safe. That belief made him more sensitive to possible signs of threat in the world around him. He noticed men lingering near doorways, watched people’s hands, and braced when anyone shifted quickly beside him. Comments about family started to feel loaded, not neutral, because they seemed to bring him too close to what had happened to his brother. In this way, what he believed about himself and his body sharpened the very things that now set him off.

Being set off so easily changed how he lived. Liam is unemployed, and much of his day is spent at home, where being left alone in a room feels intolerable because there is nothing to interrupt the flashbacks once they start. If his wife goes out, he follows her from room to room beforehand or asks if he can come along, not because he wants company in any ordinary sense, but because solitude leaves too much space for the images and smells to return. He stopped watching television and avoids films, news reports, or online clips that might show violence or injured bodies; even the possibility of seeing something similar feels dangerous. On his worst nights, when he cannot sleep and the tension in him keeps building, he has hurt himself physically to release the pressure and to break the sense that he is trapped in the memory.

These strategies have narrowed his life, and they have not brought the relief he hoped for. Avoiding television means he remains on edge about what might appear if it is turned on somewhere else, and being unable to tolerate time alone has made him more dependent on his wife in ways that embarrass him. He once saw himself as someone capable and self-directed, and now each workaround seems to confirm the opposite: that he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him and cannot rely on himself to cope. The more he pulls away from reminders and from being by himself, the less chance he has to discover that the memory might settle. Instead, the images stay raw and sensory, ready to return in fragments.

The cycle has tightened over time. Poor sleep leaves him jumpy the next day; sudden movements by other people register instantly, and once he is on guard he starts scanning for more signs that something bad is about to happen. That state makes family-related comments or suspicious behavior stand out even more, and then the smell and snapshots break through again. In response he doubles down on staying close to others, avoiding media, and trying anything to shut the reactions down, but this only keeps the memory unprocessed and his alarm system primed.

He sought help after his wife told him she was frightened by how desperate he looked when she tried to leave him alone one evening, and by the bruises he admitted giving himself after another sleepless night. Liam said he is terrified that this is permanent—that his body will keep acting as if the attack is still happening and that he will never again be the husband or brother he was before. At the same time, he is hoping, cautiously, that if he can finally make sense of what happened, he might stop living as though danger is waiting in every movement around him.
